title: NURS 1017 Unit 6 Case Study 6
description: 68-year-old male client, a retired carpenter with obesity, with osteoarthritis of the right knee and Heberden nodes; cartilage loss, bone remodeling and secondary synovitis, acetaminophen overuse and fall risk, self-management teaching, and nursing care and evaluation after a total knee arthroplasty.

authorReview.note:
New case written by Claude on 14 Oct 2026 to fill a Unit 6 gap; please review before using it with students:
Screen 3: acetaminophen maximum stated as 4 g/day, lower (often 3 g or less) for older adults and regular alcohol use; adjust to your course's reference.
Screen 4: the “1 kg lost = about 4 kg less load on the knee” figure comes from Messier et al. (2005).
Screen 6: knee flexion goal at 6 weeks (about 90°–110°) varies by surgeon.

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Nurses' Notes. Highlight the findings that are consistent with osteoarthritis or increase the client's risk for it.

highlightTabs.title: Nurses' Notes
highlightTabs.content: Day 1 1000:Retired carpenter who knelt on job sites for 40 years. Reports 3 years of {right knee pain that worsens with walking and climbing stairs and eases with rest|correct}, worse by the end of the day. {Morning stiffness in the knee lasting about 15 minutes.|correct} {Grating (crepitus) felt and heard when the right knee bends.|correct} {Hard, bony enlargements on the end joints (DIP) of both index fingers.|correct} {Weight 102 kg, BMI 33.|correct} {MCP joints and wrists not swollen or warm.} {Temperature 36.7° C.} {Reports good appetite with no weight loss.} Right knee slightly enlarged and bony, with a small cool effusion; flexion limited to 100°. {Takes ramipril 10 mg daily for hypertension.} Lives with his wife in a two-storey house.

question.explanation:
Consistent with osteoarthritis (OA):

Pain with use that eases with rest and worsens through the day: the damaged joint surfaces hurt under load. In late disease pain may also occur at rest and at night.

Short morning stiffness (usually under 30 minutes) after rest, which loosens with movement.

Crepitus: grating from roughened cartilage and bone surfaces moving against each other.

Heberden nodes: bony enlargements (osteophytes) of the distal interphalangeal joints; Bouchard nodes affect the proximal interphalangeal joints.

Risk factors: obesity (more load on weight-bearing joints, plus inflammatory substances from fat tissue) and years of repeated kneeling or joint stress. Age and previous joint injury are other major risk factors.

Not OA cues: unswollen MCP joints and wrists, a normal temperature and no weight loss argue against an inflammatory, systemic arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis. Ramipril treats his hypertension.

question.stem: The nurse is explaining the client's X-ray to him. For each finding, click to specify whether it is mainly the result of loss of articular cartilage, bone remodeling, or secondary synovial inflammation.

rows.text: Narrowing of the medial joint space
Small, cool effusion that increases after a long walk

question.explanation:
Loss of articular cartilage is the central change in OA. Chondrocytes fail to keep up with the breakdown of the cartilage matrix (driven by mechanical load and enzymes), so the cartilage softens, fissures and wears away. The joint space on X-ray is the cartilage, so its narrowing (here on the medial side, which carries the most load) shows cartilage loss.

Bone remodeling: as cartilage is lost, the bone underneath takes the load. It thickens and becomes dense (subchondral sclerosis), and joint fluid forced into cracks forms cysts. At the joint margins, new bone grows as spurs (osteophytes), which limit motion and, in the fingers, form Heberden and Bouchard nodes.

Secondary synovial inflammation: fragments of cartilage irritate the synovium, which produces a mild, cool effusion after activity. This inflammation is local and mild, so the ESR and CRP are normal and the RF is negative, unlike in rheumatoid arthritis. The normal uric acid argues against gout.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The nurse's priority concern is the client's risk for [[drop0]], because [[drop1]]. The nurse also identifies a risk for [[drop2]] related to [[drop3]].

options.text: gastrointestinal bleeding
kidney stones
liver injury
his morning stiffness lasts 15 minutes
he takes about 6.6 g of acetaminophen a day, drinks alcohol daily, and his ALT is elevated
his blood pressure is 144/88 mm Hg
pressure injury
falls
infection
his age alone
the night-time cold and flu tablet
knee instability and pain without a walking aid

question.explanation:
Liver injury: 2 × 500 mg six times a day (6 g) plus 650 mg at night is about 6.6 g of acetaminophen a day, well above the usual maximum of 4 g a day (lower, often 3 g or less, for older adults and people who drink alcohol regularly). Alcohol depletes glutathione, which the liver needs to detoxify an acetaminophen metabolite, so the risk of liver injury rises. His raised ALT is already a warning. Hidden acetaminophen in combination cold and flu products is a common cause of accidental overdose. The nurse reports this to the provider at once.

Not the priority: he is not taking NSAIDs and denies dark stools, so GI bleeding is not suggested; blood pressure and stiffness need follow-up but are not urgent.

Falls: a knee that “gives way” (from pain, quadriceps weakness and joint instability) on the stairs, without a walking aid, puts him at high risk of a fall and fracture. Age adds to the risk but is not the cause here. The cold and flu tablet may cause drowsiness, but the knee instability is the main factor.

question.stem: The nurse is planning teaching for the client. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Read the labels of all over-the-counter products for acetaminophen and keep the total within the daily limit your provider sets
Use a cane in your right hand
Rest the knee completely until the pain goes away
Do low-impact exercise such as swimming or cycling, and quadriceps-strengthening exercises
Sleep with a pillow under the right knee
Strengthen the knee with deep squats and kneeling exercises
Losing even a small amount of weight reduces the load on your knees
Apply warmth before activity to ease stiffness, and a cold pack after activity if the knee swells
Use a cane in your left hand

question.explanation:
Correct: checking labels prevents hidden acetaminophen overdose. A cane is held in the hand opposite the affected knee and moved forward with it, which shifts weight off the painful knee and widens the base of support. Heat relaxes muscles and eases stiffness before activity; cold reduces swelling and pain after activity. Low-impact aerobic exercise and quadriceps strengthening stabilize the knee and reduce pain without overloading it. Every kilogram of weight lost removes about 4 kg of load from the knee with each step.

Incorrect: a cane on the same side as the bad knee does not unload it. Complete rest causes stiffness, muscle weakness and further loss of function. Deep squats and kneeling load the damaged cartilage heavily. A pillow under the knee is comfortable but encourages a flexion contracture.

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether it is indicated, contraindicated, or nonessential for the client on postoperative day 1.

rows.text: Place a pillow under the right knee to relieve pain
Assess circulation, movement, and sensation of the right foot regularly
Encourage ankle pumps every hour while awake and keep the sequential compression devices on in bed
Keep the client on bed rest for the first 3 days
Give the prescribed analgesic before physiotherapy
Apply the prescribed cold therapy to the right knee

question.explanation:
Indicated: neurovascular checks detect nerve or vascular injury and compartment problems early. Ankle pumps and sequential compression devices promote venous return and help prevent deep vein thrombosis, a major risk after knee replacement. Pain relief before physiotherapy lets him take part in early walking and range-of-motion exercise. Cold therapy reduces swelling and pain.

Contraindicated: a pillow under the knee holds it flexed and can cause a flexion contracture; the knee is kept straight when resting (a pillow may go under the calf and heel if the leg is elevated). Bed rest increases the risk of blood clots, pneumonia and stiffness; walking usually starts on the day of surgery or the day after.

Nonessential: hand X-rays do not change his postoperative care.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it indicates that the plan of care has been effective or not effective.

rows.text: Right knee flexion 105° with full extension
Warm, swollen, tender right calf, 3 cm larger than the left
Walks with a cane in his left hand, with no falls
“I still sleep with a pillow under my right knee.”
Incision healed, with no redness or drainage
“I check labels and keep track of my acetaminophen.”

question.explanation:
Effective: good range of motion (about 90° to 110° of flexion is a usual goal at this stage), a healed incision, safe use of the cane on the correct side with no falls, weight loss, and safe use of acetaminophen.

Not effective: a warm, swollen, tender calf that is larger than the other suggests a deep vein thrombosis, which can lead to a pulmonary embolism. The nurse does not massage the calf, has the client rest, and reports the finding to the provider immediately. Sleeping with a pillow under the knee risks a flexion contracture and loss of the extension gained in therapy; the nurse reteaches keeping the knee straight.
